blocks.title: 1.1 Problem Statement
blocks.body:
Non-Deterministic Finite Automata (NFAs) offer an intuitive and expressive mathematical framework for modeling regular languages, enabling state transitions to branch simultaneously across multiple paths or terminate on dead ends. However, physical computer hardware and production lexers/compilers are deterministic systems that cannot pursue multiple execution paths concurrently. Consequently, NFAs must be systematically converted into equivalent Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs).

In university Automata Theory curricula, the Subset Construction (Rabin-Scott powerset construction) is the fundamental bridge connecting non-determinism to deterministic realization. However, students frequently encounter significant pedagogical hurdles: (1) visualizing how multiple concurrent NFA states coalesce into a single composite DFA state, (2) tracking non-trivial state-space blowup (up to 2ⁿ states), (3) comprehending why dead states (∅) are necessary for total transition functions, and (4) verifying whether the generated DFA rigorously accepts the exact same language as the original NFA. Existing software often presents conversion as a single 'black-box' step, depriving learners of the incremental, step-by-step mathematical union derivation required for viva examinations.

blocks.title: 1.2 Project Objectives
blocks.body:
The primary goal of this project is to design and develop “Automata Workbench” — a transparent, educational, interactive Python simulator specifically tailored for Topic 1: NFA → DFA Conversion. The project targets the following measurable objectives:
1. Step-by-Step Pedagogical Visualization: Provide an interactive construction player (Reset, Step Prev, Step Next, Auto-Play) that displays the exact mathematical union δ(q, a) computed at each transition step.
2. Dual-Machine Simultaneous Verification: Simulate user-entered strings simultaneously on both the NFA and DFA, displaying step-by-step active state frontiers and proving language equivalence through automated agreement verification.
3. Strict Architectural Purity for Viva Defense: Completely isolate all automata mathematics in a pure-Python package (`algorithm/`) containing zero UI or framework dependencies, heavily commented in beginner-friendly English so that student teams can explain every line during academic vivas.
4. Client-Side Rendering with Zero System Footprint: Dynamically synthesize Graphviz DOT code rendered natively in the browser without requiring external C-libraries, binaries, or cloud dependencies.

blocks.title: 1.3 System Inputs & Outputs
blocks.body:
• System Inputs:
   - States Q: Comma-separated list of alphanumeric state identifiers (e.g., q0, q1, q2; capped at 12 states).
   - Alphabet Σ: Comma-separated single-character input tokens (e.g., a, b or 0, 1).
   - Start State q₀: Exactly one state selected from Q.
   - Accepting States F: Subset of states F ⊆ Q.
   - Transition Table δ_NFA: Matrix specifying target states for each (state, symbol) pair via multi-select choice or text input.
   - Verification Strings w: Individual strings or batch newline-delimited test suites for language verification.

• System Outputs:
   - Complete DFA Specification: States Q_DFA, Alphabet Σ, Transition function δ_DFA, Start state q₀_DFA, Accepts F_DFA.
   - Canonical Subset Mapping: Transparent correspondence between alphabetical aliases (A, B, C...) and exact subsets ({q0}, {q0,q1}).
   - Visual State Diagrams: Interactive Graphviz diagrams for both machines with double-circle accept states and subset highlighting.
   - Step Construction Log: Chronological natural language log explaining the origin, symbol, move union, and result state for each step.
   - Trace & Agreement Report: Step-by-step state execution path and automated verification confirmation showing NFA and DFA equivalence.

blocks.title: 1.4 Formal Mathematical Specification
blocks.body:
• Formal Definition of the Input NFA:
The input machine is formally specified as a 5-tuple:
      M_NFA = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)
Where:
   1. Q is a finite non-empty set of states: Q = {q₀, q₁, ..., qₙ₋₁}, with |Q| ≤ 12.
   2. Σ is a finite non-empty input alphabet such that ∀a ∈ Σ, |a| = 1 and a ∉ {ε, eps, epsilon, λ, lambda}.
   3. δ: Q × Σ → 𝒫(Q) is the transition function mapping each state and symbol to a subset of Q. Note that δ(q, a) = ∅ indicates no valid transition.
   4. q₀ ∈ Q is the designated initial state.
   5. F ⊆ Q is the set of final/accepting states.

• Formal Definition of the Target DFA:
The resulting converted deterministic machine is specified as:
      M_DFA = (Q', Σ, δ', q₀', F')
Where:
   1. Q' ⊆ 𝒫(Q) is the set of reachable subsets of Q discovered during powerset exploration (|Q'| ≤ 2^|Q|).
   2. Σ is identical to the input NFA alphabet.
   3. q₀' = {q₀} is the DFA start state, consisting of the singleton set containing the NFA start state.
   4. δ': Q' × Σ → Q' is the deterministic total transition function defined mathematically by:
            δ'(S, a) = ⋃_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a)   for all S ∈ Q' and a ∈ Σ
      If ⋃_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a) = ∅, the transition lands in the explicit dead/trap state ∅, where δ'(∅, a) = ∅ for all a ∈ Σ.
   5. F' = {S ∈ Q' | S ∩ F ≠ ∅} is the set of DFA accepting states (a subset state is accepting iff it contains at least one NFA accepting state).

• Language Equivalence Theorem:
The subset construction guarantees that L(M_NFA) = L(M_DFA). An input string w = a₁a₂...aₘ is accepted by M_NFA iff there exists a path q₀ → q₁ → ... → qₘ such that qₘ ∈ F. By induction on |w|, the state S reached by M_DFA on input w is precisely the set of all NFA states reachable from q₀ on input w. Therefore, S ∈ F' if and only if S ∩ F ≠ ∅, proving rigorous language equivalence.

• Scope Boundaries:
- Plain NFAs only: ε-transitions are intentionally excluded (ε-NFA is a separate curricular topic). Friendly validation errors reject any attempt to input ε.
- Upper State Bound: Maximum 12 NFA states to prevent uncontrolled exponential explosion in educational environments (2¹² = 4096 states).

blocks.title: 2.1 Review of Existing Tools
blocks.body:
To establish a solid rationale for designing a new simulator, existing academic and open-source automata tools were reviewed:

1. JFLAP (Java Formal Languages and Automata Package):
   - Background: Developed at Duke University, JFLAP is the historical gold standard for teaching automata theory.
   - Limitations: Built on legacy Java Swing architecture; requires a local Java Runtime Environment (JRE) install which frequently causes modern OS security and DPI scaling issues. Graph layout often requires manual node dragging. Critically, JFLAP's conversion utility generates dense, cluttered transition tables without clear natural language step explanations or synchronized dual-machine frontier tracing.

2. Python Computational Libraries (Automata-lib, FAdo):
   - Background: Pure Python and C++ libraries designed for programmatic automata minimization, regex parsing, and union operations.
   - Limitations: Strictly developer-oriented CLI tools without a visual user interface. They perform conversions as instantaneous batch operations, providing zero visual intermediate steps for students learning how the algorithm functions.

3. Generic Web-Based State Machine Editors (e.g., FSM Simulator, Cyberzhg):
   - Background: JavaScript/Canvas-based web apps allowing users to draw graphs in the browser.
   - Limitations: Most online tools combine ε-transitions, DFA minimization, and regex conversion into a single monolithic interface. They lack structured validation, do not support interactive step-by-step subset construction playback, and do not provide side-by-side verification proving that the generated DFA agrees with the NFA.

blocks.title: 2.3 Feasibility Analysis
blocks.body:
• Technical Feasibility: Highly Feasible. The technology stack relies solely on Python ≥ 3.10 and Streamlit ≥ 1.40. Crucially, Graphviz DOT text is rendered client-side directly by the browser using Streamlit's built-in `st.graphviz_chart()`. This completely eliminates the need for OS-level Graphviz binary installations (`dot` executable) or C-extensions, ensuring 100% platform portability across Windows, macOS, and Linux.

• Pedagogical & Operational Feasibility: Highly Feasible. The user experience is optimized for classroom demos and viva presentations. Preloaded with thirteen verified presets plus a blank Custom mode (including famous edge cases such as 'Ends with ab', '3rd symbol from end is a' state blow-up, 'Dead state ∅' and the unary mod-2-or-3 union), students can immediately explore the algorithm without tedious manual setup. The strict separation of pure-Python automata logic in `algorithm/` ensures students can confidently read, explain, and defend every mathematical function.

• Economic & Resource Feasibility: Highly Feasible. All components are free, open-source software (MIT/Apache licenses). The simulator executes entirely locally on commodity consumer laptops with zero cloud infrastructure, hosting, or database expenses.

blocks.title: 3.1 High-Level Architecture & Separation of Concerns
blocks.body:
The simulator adopts a strict decoupled architecture comprising two independent layers:
1. Pure Computational Logic Layer (`algorithm/`): Contains zero UI code, zero Streamlit imports, and zero third-party dependencies. All data structures are implemented using standard library dataclasses. This guarantees that the core automata engine can be tested, verified, and explained completely independently in terminal environments via `algorithm.demo`.
2. Presentation & Interaction Layer (`app.py`, `ui/`): A thin reactive controller that handles session state, form validation reporting, Graphviz DOT synthesis (`ui/graphs.py`), and the light/dark theme stylesheet (`ui/styles.py`).

blocks.title: 4.1 Algorithm Selection & Justification
blocks.body:
The project implements the Rabin-Scott Powerset / Subset Construction using Breadth-First Search (BFS) queue exploration. This algorithm is selected over naive brute-force powerset generation for several vital reasons:
1. Minimal Reachable Subgraph: An NFA with n states has 2ⁿ potential subsets. Brute-force generation constructs all 2ⁿ states indiscriminately. In contrast, the BFS queue approach explores only reachable subsets starting from {q₀}, eliminating disconnected unreachable states and keeping the DFA as compact as possible.
2. Deterministic Canonical Ordering: By sorting and de-duplicating subset members based on their initial NFA declaration order, the subset string ID (e.g. {q0,q1}) and assigned alias (A, B, C...) are 100% deterministic and reproducible across repeated runs.
3. Total DFA Transition Guarantee: When transitions for certain symbols do not exist in the NFA, the algorithm maps them to the explicit dead/trap state ∅, ensuring the output strictly satisfies the formal definition of a total DFA.

blocks.title: 4.2 Structured Algorithmic Pseudocode
blocks.body:
Algorithm: SubsetConstruction(NFA)
Input:  NFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)
Output: DFA M' = (Q', Σ, δ', q₀', F') and ConstructionLog Steps
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Let Order = map assigning declaration index to each q ∈ Q
2.  Define Normalize(S): return sorted unique elements of S ordered by Order
3.  Define SetID(S): if S is empty return '∅', else return '{' + join(S, ',') + '}'
4.  Let KnownStates = empty dictionary {SetID -> DFAState}
5.  Let DFAStatesList = empty list
6.  Let DFATransitions = empty nested dictionary {SetID -> {symbol -> SetID}}
7.  Let StepsLog = empty list
8.  
9.  Function RegisterState(members):
10.     sid = SetID(members)
11.     if sid in KnownStates: return KnownStates[sid]
12.     alias = AliasFor(length of DFAStatesList)   // 0->A, 1->B...
13.     is_acc = (members ∩ F ≠ ∅)
14.     is_dead = (length of members == 0)
15.     state = CreateDFAState(id=sid, alias=alias, members=members, is_acc, is_dead)
16.     KnownStates[sid] = state
17.     Append state to DFAStatesList
18.     DFATransitions[sid] = empty dictionary
19.     return state
20. 
21. // Step 1: Initialize start state
22. start_state = RegisterState(Normalize([q₀]))
23. start_state.is_start = True
24. 
25. // Step 2: Breadth-first queue processing
26. Queue = FIFOQueue([start_state])
27. while Queue is not empty:
28.     Current = Queue.pop_left()
29.     for each symbol a ∈ Σ:
30.         moves = []
31.         for each q ∈ Current.members:
32.             targets = Normalize(δ(q, a))
33.             moves.append(MoveDetail(state=q, targets=targets))
34.         
35.         // Compute Union: T = ⋃ δ(q, a)
36.         result_members = Normalize(⋃ move.targets)
37.         prev_count = length of KnownStates
38.         target_state = RegisterState(result_members)
39.         is_new = (length of KnownStates > prev_count)
40.         if is_new:
41.             Queue.push(target_state)  // Enqueue newly discovered subset
42.         
43.         DFATransitions[Current.id][a] = target_state.id
44.         StepsLog.append(ConstructionStep(Current, a, moves, result_members, target_state, is_new))
45. 
46. Return DFA(states=DFAStatesList, alphabet=Σ, transitions=DFATransitions, start=start_state.id, accepts), StepsLog

blocks.title: 4.3 Manually Solved Validation Example (Walkthrough)

blocks.text:
• Manual String Verification & Language Equivalence:
   - String 'ab':
       DFA Path: A ──a──► B ──b──► C (Accepting) ──► ACCEPTED
       NFA Active Frontier: [q0] ──a──► [q0, q1] ──b──► [q0, q2] (contains q2) ──► ACCEPTED (Agreement ✓)
   - String 'aab':
       DFA Path: A ──a──► B ──a──► B ──b──► C (Accepting) ──► ACCEPTED
       NFA Active Frontier: [q0] ──a──► [q0, q1] ──a──► [q0, q1] ──b──► [q0, q2] ──► ACCEPTED (Agreement ✓)
   - String 'abb':
       DFA Path: A ──a──► B ──b──► C ──b──► A (Non-accepting) ──► REJECTED
       NFA Active Frontier: [q0] ──a──► [q0, q1] ──b──► [q0, q2] ──b──► [q0] (no q2) ──► REJECTED (Agreement ✓)
   - String ε (empty):
       DFA State: A (Non-accepting) ──► REJECTED
       NFA State: q0 ∉ F ──► REJECTED (Agreement ✓)

blocks.title: 5. Plain-Language Walkthrough (How to Explain This Project)
5.1 The idea in four sentences
blocks.body:
1. An NFA may be in several states at once and may have no move at all; a DFA must be in exactly one state and always have a move.
2. Both machines accept exactly the same class of languages (regular languages), so every NFA can be converted into a DFA.
3. The trick is to let each DFA state be a set of NFA states, namely 'every place the NFA could be right now'.
4. Our simulator starts with {start}, applies each symbol, collects the union of all reachable NFA states, and repeats until no new sets appear.

blocks.title: 5.2 Everyday analogy
blocks.body: Imagine following a rumour in a town. A non-deterministic rumour can reach several people at once. Instead of tracking each person separately, the DFA keeps one note that says 'the rumour is currently with {Asha, Ravi}'. After each new word (input symbol) the note is rewritten with the new list of people. Each distinct note becomes one DFA state. The rumour 'succeeds' if the note ever contains a person marked as the goal (an accepting NFA state).

blocks.title: 5.4 Questions an examiner may ask
blocks.body:
Q: Why can the DFA have up to 2ⁿ states? A: Each DFA state is a subset of the n NFA states, and there are 2ⁿ subsets. The preset '2nd symbol from the end is 1' shows this growth.
Q: Why do we only build reachable subsets? A: The BFS queue starts at {q0} and only enqueues sets it actually reaches, so unreachable subsets are never created.
Q: What happens when an NFA state has no move on a symbol? A: Its contribution to the union is empty; if the whole union is empty the DFA moves to the dead state ∅, which loops on every symbol.
Q: How do you know the DFA is correct? A: Section 4.3 verifies four strings by hand, and the app runs every test string on both machines and shows an agreement badge; 59 automated tests also cover this.
Q: Why no ε-transitions? A: The specification (Section 1.4) covers NFAs without ε; ε-closure would be a documented extension.

blocks.title: 5.5 Preliminary prototype status
blocks.body: A working prototype already exists (python -m streamlit run app.py inside nfa2dfa-simulator/). It implements everything in this design: editor with 13 presets and a blank custom mode, live NFA and DFA diagrams, step player with construction log, NFA/DFA transition tables, single and batch string testing, JSON export of the DFA, and a light/dark theme. The 59 automated tests pass. The report therefore describes a design that has already been validated in code.

blocks.title: Conclusion & Next Steps for Milestone 2
blocks.body: The theoretical design, mathematical specification, architecture, and manual verification for Milestone 1 are complete. As established in the feasibility study, the project methodology provides a deterministic, reliable foundation for implementation. A preliminary prototype (Section 5.5) already implements this design and passes its 59-test suite. Milestone 2 will focus on polishing, extended presets, and optional ε-NFA support.
